overview.intro: Economics argues in words and proves in numbers, and statistics is the bridge between the two. This unit covers the definition and scope of statistics together with the limitations that make a careless figure dangerous, the methods of collecting and presenting data, the measures of central value and dispersion that summarise a distribution, correlation and index numbers, and the mathematical tools economics uses. Every figure in this chapter is computed here so that the method can be followed rather than memorised.

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: Statistics is the collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation of quantitative data.

facts.label: Central values
facts.value: Mean, median and mode, each answering a slightly different question about the centre of a distribution.

facts.label: Dispersion
facts.value: Range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation measure spread about the centre.

facts.label: Tools
facts.value: Correlation measures association, index numbers measure change over time, and algebra and graphs carry the reasoning.

learn.title: Definition, scope and limitations of statistics

blocks.text: Statistics may be defined as the collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation of quantitative data. Four elements are involved. Collection means gathering facts with a clear purpose and suitable methods. Presentation means arranging the data in a form that can be understood, such as tables, bar diagrams and pie charts. Analysis means applying measures such as averages and dispersion to extract meaning. Interpretation means drawing conclusions from the results in the light of the problem being studied. The word quantitative is essential: statistics deals with data that can be measured and expressed in numbers.

blocks.text: Data may be collected directly or indirectly. Direct methods are interviews, questionnaires, schedules and personal observation, which give accurate and current information but are expensive and slow. Indirect methods use records already kept, such as government reports, company accounts and registration data, which are cheap and quick but may be outdated or incomplete. Secondary data must be checked for the source, the definition used, the period covered and the method of collection before it is relied upon.

Presentation turns raw figures into a readable form. A textual presentation describes in sentences, a tabular presentation arranges data in rows and columns with clear headings and units, and a diagrammatic presentation uses bar charts, pie charts and line graphs. The choice depends on the audience: a table for precise values, a bar diagram for comparison between categories, a pie chart for proportions of a whole, and a line graph for change over time.

learn.title: Measures of central value: mean, median and mode

blocks.text: The mean, or arithmetic average, is the sum of the values divided by their number of observations. It uses every observation and is therefore the most representative for further calculation, but it is badly affected by a few extreme values. The median is the middle value when the observations are arranged in order, and it is unaffected by extreme values, which makes it the better measure for skewed data such as incomes. The mode is the value that occurs most frequently, and it is useful when the most common item matters, such as the most common shoe size sold.

Worked example: for the data 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 30 the mean is 142 divided by 7, which is 20.29. The median is the fourth value in the ordered list, which is 20. There is no repeated value, so no mode exists in this set. With an even number of observations the median is the average of the two middle values, for example the median of 4, 7, 9, 12 is 8.

Mode is 40, which is exactly what a shopkeeper needs for stock planning.

blocks.text: A central value alone is dangerous, because two distributions can share a mean and be entirely different in spread. Dispersion measures the degree of variation around the centre. The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values and is quick but says nothing about the values between. The quartile deviation is half the interquartile range and is unaffected by extremes. Mean deviation takes the average of the absolute deviations from a central value. Standard deviation, the square root of the average of squared deviations from the mean, is the most used measure because it is mathematically tractable and forms the basis of further analysis.

Worked example: for 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 30 the mean is 20.29 and the standard deviation is the square root of the average of the squared deviations. The squared deviations are 68.6, 28.0, 5.3, 0.08, 2.9, 22.2 and 94.3, which sum to 221.4; dividing by 7 gives 31.6 and the square root is 5.62. A coefficient of variation expresses this as a percentage of the mean, giving 5.62 divided by 20.29 times 100, which is 27.7 per cent, so that two series of different units can be compared.

learn.title: Correlation, index numbers and mathematical tools

blocks.text: Correlation measures the degree of association between two variables. A positive correlation means the variables move in the same direction, as height and weight generally do; a negative correlation means they move in opposite directions, as price and quantity demanded usually do; and zero correlation means no linear relationship. The coefficient runs from minus one to plus one, and its value measures strength as well as direction. Correlation describes association only, and a high coefficient never by itself proves that one variable causes the other.

An index number measures the change in a variable or a set of variables over time, taking a base period value of one hundred. A price index measured at 125 means prices are 25 per cent above the base year. The consumer price index is built from a weighted basket of goods, where weights reflect the share of each item in total expenditure, so that a rise in an item families actually buy heavily counts more than a rise in a rare purchase. Inflation is then calculated as the percentage change in the index between two periods.

keyPoints: Statistics is the collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation of quantitative data.
Its limitations are that it deals only with quantitative facts, that averages are true on average, and that carelessness misleads.
Data collection is direct through interviews and schedules or indirect through existing records.
Presentation is textual, tabular or diagrammatic, chosen for the audience.
Mean uses every observation but is distorted by extremes; median and mode are resistant to them.
Standard deviation is the square root of the mean of squared deviations from the mean.
The coefficient of variation compares spread between series of different units.
Correlation measures association from minus one to plus one and never proves causation.
An index number measures change over time with the base period set at 100.
Weights in an index reflect each item’s share in total expenditure.
examFocus: Numerical questions must show the formula, the substitution and the unit of the answer, since method carries marks.
When mean and median are both asked for, give both and say which better describes the given data and why.
In index number questions state the base year and the weights, because an index without them cannot be interpreted.

questions.prompt: The measure of central value unaffected by a few extreme observations is:
questions.explanation: The median depends only on position in the ordered series, so an extreme value cannot pull it away from the centre.

questions.prompt: For the data 10, 12, 12, 15, 20 the mean is:
questions.explanation: The values sum to 69 and there are five observations, so 69 divided by 5 gives 13.8.

options: Prices are 130 per cent lower than the base year
Prices are 30 per cent above the base year
questions.answer: Prices are 30 per cent above the base year
questions.explanation: The index is read against a base of 100, so 130 indicates a rise of 30 per cent over the base period.

questions.prompt: A correlation coefficient of minus 0.9 between price and quantity demanded indicates:
options: A strong negative association, not proof of causation
That price causes quantity with certainty
questions.answer: A strong negative association, not proof of causation
questions.explanation: The value is close to minus one, showing a strong inverse association, but correlation alone never establishes causation.

questions.prompt: The square root of the mean of the squared deviations from the mean is the __________ deviation.
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the most widely used measure of spread because it suits further statistical analysis.

questions.prompt: The measure of variation that expresses standard deviation as a percentage of the mean is the coefficient of __________ .
questions.explanation: The coefficient of variation allows two series measured in different units or at different levels to be compared.

questions.answer: Four limitations are: statistics deals only with quantitative facts and cannot measure qualitative attributes such as happiness; statistical conclusions are true for the group as a whole and not necessarily for any individual member; figures collected carelessly or with a hidden definition mislead more than they inform; and correlation shows association without proving that one variable causes the other. Dependence on the choice of definition and base period is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each limitation needs a line of explanation or an illustration, since a bare list earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between mean and median on three bases.
questions.answer: On calculation, the mean is the sum of the observations divided by their number, while the median is the middle value of the series after arranging it in order. On sensitivity, the mean is pulled by extreme values, whereas the median is unaffected by them. On use, the mean is preferred where further arithmetic is required and the data are fairly symmetrical, while the median is preferred for skewed data such as wages or incomes. For an even number of observations the median is taken as the average of the two middle values.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are required, each drawn as a contrast rather than a description of one measure.

questions.prompt: Define statistics, state its scope, and explain the measures of central value with the circumstances in which each is used.
questions.answer: Statistics is the collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation of quantitative data. Its scope covers the study of economic and social facts in numerical form, the comparison between groups and over time, the measurement of relationships between variables, and its role as the basis of planning, forecasting and policy. Its limitations are that it deals only with quantitative facts, that its conclusions hold for the group rather than for every member, and that careless collection produces misleading results. The mean is the arithmetic average, found by dividing the sum of observations by their number, and is used when the data are fairly symmetrical and further calculation is needed, since it uses every observation. The median is the middle value of the ordered series and is used for skewed data such as incomes because extreme values cannot move it. The mode is the most frequent value and is used when the most common item matters, such as the shoe size most often sold. Where two series must be compared, the measures of dispersion such as standard deviation and the coefficient of variation are reported alongside the centre.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the definition, scope, limitations and all three measures with the situation that suits each.

questions.prompt: A trader reports the wages 10, 12, 12, 13 and 40 (in thousands) as showing a healthy average wage of 17.4 thousand. Evaluate the claim using measures of central value and dispersion and state what should be reported instead.
questions.answer: The arithmetic mean is indeed 87 divided by 5, which is 17.4 thousand, so the trader’s figure is correct as arithmetic. It is however a poor description of these wages, because the single value of 40 pulls the mean well above four of the five observations. The median is 12 thousand, and the mode is also 12 thousand, both of which show what a typical worker in this group actually earns. The dispersion confirms the problem: the range is 30 thousand, from 10 to 40, which is more than twice the median itself, so the wages are widely spread rather than comfortably clustered. The trader should report the median as the typical wage, with the range or standard deviation to show the spread, and mention the mean only with a note that it is affected by the highest earner. The lesson is that a healthy-looking average can be produced by one outlier, and a claim about typical wages should rest on a resistant measure.
questions.explanation: The answer is marked on computing correctly, identifying the outlier effect, and specifying a better reporting convention rather than merely saying the average is misleading.
